transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I... I came in because things just aren't right up here lately. I've been working at the library for years, you know, doing the cataloguing, keeping everything in its proper place. It’s a quiet job, which I usually like, but lately... lately it’s like my mind is just completely bogged down in this thick, heavy fog. I sit down at my desk, and I look at my old cataloguing notes—notes I wrote myself, mind you, just a few weeks ago—and I can't even keep my place. I read the same line over and over, and the words just slide right off my brain. And it’s not just the reading. It’s the deciding. I’ll finish one stack of books, and then I just sit there, staring at the cart, completely unable to figure out what simple thing I should do next. Should I start the fiction section? Should I check the returns? It’s like the gears are rusted shut, and I just can't make a choice. I used to be so sharp, so organized, but now it takes me ten minutes just to figure out where to put a single biography, and... well, it’s just very frustrating, and honestly, a bit frightening, to feel like you can't even trust your own head to do the simplest tasks anymore.
Can you tell me if, besides the difficulty concentrating and making decisions, you’ve also been feeling down, sad, or have lost interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy?

Well, yes... yes, that's exactly it. It’s like you took the words right out of my mouth. I was just thinking about this the other morning, actually. I always wake up early—it's a habit from my years at the library, you know, getting in before the doors open to sort the overnight returns—so I get up, and I sit at my kitchen table. It's a nice old oak table, very sturdy, had it for decades. But most days lately, I just sit there with my coffee, and I look around, and... I don't know how else to describe it except to say it feels like all the color has just completely gone out of everything. 

The whole world just looks washed out and gray to me now. And it’s not just how things look, it’s how I feel about the things I usually love. Like my painting. I’ve always been big into watercolors in my spare time—landscapes, mostly, some botanical stuff—and I have these old watercolor books that I’ve collected over the years. Beautiful instructional books. I used to spend my whole weekend just studying the washes and the brush techniques, getting lost in the process. It was my favorite thing to do. 

But now... now I look over at those books sitting on the shelf, and instead of feeling interested or inspired, I just feel... heavy. Just this awful, sinking heaviness in my chest. I don't even want to pick them up. It’s like the thought of even opening the cover is just too much effort, and there's no joy left in it anyway. I just sit there at the kitchen table staring at them, feeling completely empty, and it goes on like that for hours sometimes, where I just can't seem to care about any of it... it's just a terrible way to wake up, you know, knowing the whole day is going to feel like wading through wet cement...
Have you noticed that you feel more tired or that you're lacking energy, even if you haven't done anything physically or mentally exhausting?

Well, it’s... you know, I’ve actually wondered about that myself, doctor. I’ve sat there and thought, am I just getting old? Am I just physically worn out? But when I really stop and take stock of it, no, I don't think that's it at all. Physically speaking, my body feels perfectly fine. I still do my morning walk to the library—it’s exactly one point two miles from my front porch, straight down Elm Street, right past where that old bakery used to be before they turned it into a hardware store a couple of years back. I walk that every single morning, rain or shine, and my legs don't ache, my breathing is perfectly steady. I'm not winded, I don't feel like I need to go lie down and take a nap in the middle of the afternoon or anything like that. 

It’s not like I’ve been out in the yard digging ditches or chopping wood, either. My job is mostly sitting at the desk, maybe pushing a book cart here and there, and Dave, our maintenance man, just oiled the wheels on all the metal carts last month, so they glide right along with barely a push. So, physically... no, the energy is there in my muscles. I could probably walk five miles right now if you asked me to. It’s not a tired feeling in my body, it’s just... well, like I was saying before, it’s that my brain just doesn't want to do anything with the energy I do have. So I wouldn't say I'm lacking physical energy or feeling exhausted in the way you're describing, no. It's really just that mental fog and the grayness of it all making me just sit there.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently—like not wanting to eat or losing weight without trying?

Well, yes, actually, now that you mention it, there has been a change there, too. It’s funny you ask that, because my wife, Martha—we’ve been married for thirty-eight years this coming October—she’s the one who really pointed it out to me. She’s a wonderful cook, always has been. She makes this incredible chicken noodle soup from scratch, roasts the bones and everything, and she always serves it with a nice big bowl of rice on the side. It's a staple in our house, especially when the weather starts turning a bit chilly like it has been lately. Usually, I’m the first one at the table, and I’d never, ever leave a single grain of rice in the bowl. I grew up in a house where you didn't waste food, you know? You ate what was put in front of you and you were grateful for it. 

But lately... I just don't have the drive for it. I sit down at the table, and the soup is right there, steaming and smelling just as good as it always does, but my stomach just feels... indifferent, I suppose. I'll take a few spoonfuls, maybe pick at the rice a bit, and then I just put my spoon down. Martha will look over at me and say, "Are you feeling alright? You've barely touched your dinner," and I look down and realize my bowl is still half full. I just don't feel the hunger. I honestly have to remind myself that it's time to eat, like, "Oh, it's noon, I suppose I should have a sandwich," rather than actually feeling hungry for it. It's just another thing that seems to have lost its appeal, right along with the watercolors and everything else. So, yes, I'm definitely not eating the way I used to, and I suppose if I stepped on a scale, it might show I've dropped a few pounds, just from leaving all those half-finished meals on the table.
Have you found yourself feeling hopeless or worthless lately, or have you had any thoughts about life not being worth living?

Well, no... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, it's not that I think life isn't worth living or anything drastic like that. I know some people get to that point, and I've read about it—working in a library, you come across all sorts of memoirs and psychology books, and I always make a point to skim the new arrivals before they go on the shelves. There was one just last month, a very moving account by a fellow who went through something similar, and he talked about feeling like he was just a burden to everyone, like he had no value left. But I don't feel that way. 

I know Martha needs me, and the library needs me—even if it's just to make sure the periodicals are filed correctly, because if I don't do it, they just pile up in the back room. So I know I have a purpose, and I don't feel worthless. It's really just... well, like I was trying to explain with the watercolors and the grayness of everything. It's just a profound lack of interest, a sort of... flatness. I don't sit there thinking, "Oh, woe is me, I'm no good," or "I wish I wasn't here." It's more like, "I am here, but I just can't seem to care about being here right now." 

So, no, no thoughts about not wanting to be alive or feeling like I'm completely hopeless. I know things can get better, I just... I'm just waiting for the color to come back, I suppose. I just wish I knew how long it was going to take, because sitting at that oak table every morning staring at a half-eaten bowl of oatmeal or soup or whatever Martha makes... it's just tedious, really. But no, no thoughts of giving up entirely.
Have you noticed that you're moving more slowly than usual, or that it takes you much longer to get things done, even simple tasks like getting dressed or making a cup of tea?

Well, yes, actually, now that you mention it, that is something I've noticed. It's... it's quite frustrating, to be honest with you. It's not that I don't have the energy, like I was saying before—my muscles are fine. But it's more like... like my body is just moving through molasses. 

Just the other day, I was walking down to the corner store—the one on 4th and Main, run by the Miller family, they've been there since my kids were little—just to pick up a paper. Usually, I'm out the door, down the block, and back in maybe fifteen minutes tops. But this time, it felt like every step was just... heavy. I had to consciously think about picking up my foot, moving it forward, setting it down. It took me nearly half an hour, and Mrs. Miller even asked if my arthritis was acting up, which I don't even have! 

And it's not just walking, either. It's the little things at work. I sit at my desk, and I have these stacks of periodicals to sort—magazines, journals, the daily papers. I've done it a million times, I have a whole system. But lately, I'll pick up a copy of National Geographic, and my hand just moves so slowly to put it in the right pile. It's like the signal from my brain to my hand is taking a detour or something. Martha noticed it too, when I was getting dressed for church on Sunday. I was trying to button my shirt, and my fingers were just fumbling, moving so deliberately, like I was trying to thread a needle in the dark. It just takes so much more effort than it should, you know? It's not that I can't do it, it's just that the whole process is dragged out, and I feel like I'm watching myself move in slow motion.
